utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The late start is caused by a late finish by the Chamber that previously used this courtroom. Mr. Lausic, I'd like to remind you again that the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony still binds you. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much. One quick housekeeping matter, Your Honour. There was an issue raised yesterday concerning P877. I'm advised that the translation in e-court is indeed the revised translation. I, unfortunately, had the previous translation. Should I have occasion to refer to it again, I now have the revised translation that, as indicated, is in fact in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at the portions quoted and do not think that there`s specific reason to revisit those questions again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, yesterday there were some questions and some testimony concerning the reporting system and to both the police -- the military police administration and to the Military District Commanders. I think beginning at page 15245, you began speaking about the organisational form that was set up in the operational duty section and the daily reports issued, and I believe there was an invitation to show you such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I'd like to call up D1069 and ask that it be placed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, the document that will come up on the screen is not a document that, to my knowledge, was presented to you before, although you may or may not be familiar with it, so I'll ask you to look it over now.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct I see this document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is a daily report for 2 September 1995 from the Split Military District, military post 2233, duty service. The Ministry of Defence military police administration, operations department, stamp appears on it below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we turn to page -- to the back of the document, basically, beginning at page 3 of the English and continuing, and the back of the document in Croatian, we see the indications of where that document was sent; number one, operations duty department of the military police administration; two, Split Military District Commander, and then some other addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, is --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could we please zoom in so that I could read the letters on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in the English, if we could turn to page 3, at the bottom of page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, my question, Mr. Lausic - and certainly, if you need additional time to look at the document, you will certainly be permitted to do so - is that an example of the daily reporting to which you were referring yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. This is a standard report which was to be submitted every day until 2400 hours at the latest to the duty operations section in Zagreb, based on the reports from the military police. Based on this report, the duty officer at the administration comprised daily bulletins which would early in the morning be distributed to the highest level within the Ministry of Defence, as well as to the office of the President, the chief of the Main Staff, as well as other most senior officials. This report used a standard template, which covered some specific military police segments. As I can see, some parts of the report mention no specific events, whereas some others do, and I can see that also one other standard item is present, and that is that that the military police was duty-bound to send this on a daily basis. According to the format, the chapters included, and the language used, this was a standard type of reporting that was in force during those several years, which partially included the war years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could show you one additional document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That would be 65 ter 3343.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document dated 15 November 1995 from Commander Colonel General Gotovina, signed for him, to the attention of military police post 2233, the commander Colonel Budimir, and the subject is: Submission of reports warning. The beginning of the document states: "It is the everyday practice that the daily reports of the duty service of the military post 2233 arrive in the operations centre of the Split Military District Command, Knin forward command post, with delay." It goes to on to explain that one of the reasons for that delay is the fact that the reports are addressed to the Split Military District Commander, and: "... since there is no need for that and in order to enable the officers who process the unusual incidents in the area of responsibility of the Split Military District to finish their job on time, I am asking you to address the daily reports to the operations centre of the Split Military District Command." And again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lausic, I wanted to ask you if that is a reference to and reflection of the daily reports which were sent to the Military Districts by the military police to which you referred yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific, since I am not clear as to what I should focus my response on. This is a warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah. The -- just -- I'm looking at the reference to: It is the everyday practice that the daily reports of the duty service of the military post 2233, et cetera. Is that a reference to the types of daily reports that you were speaking about yesterday that were sent to the Military Districts?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Mention is made here that it is everyday practice for the daily reports of the duty service of the military post 2233, which was the second [as interpreted] MP battalion, and that those arrive in the operations centre of the Split Military District Command, Knin forward command post with delay. Some reasons are specified for those delays, and an order is issued to address those reports to different addressees that some changes be made therein. There was no dispute about those daily reports arriving on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just say something? The transcript says "second MP Battalion". I think it should be 72nd MP Battalion. I'm sure Mr. Tieger would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's right, although my experience is that sometimes the -- what appears initially here is quickly corrected by the stenographer, but I think Mr. Kay is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was how it was translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I think it was said in English. It is not a transcribing issue, but it's, rather, either the way in which the witness expressed himself or a translation issue. But I take it that you referred to the 72nd Battalion rather than to the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I'm grateful to Mr. Kay. Can we call up 65 ter 1334, please. I'm sorry, Your Honour, and maybe it is an appropriate time, then, to tender 65 ter 3343.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is not yet on your list then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's on the list, but we can wait. However -- we can either handle it now or wait to have them tendered in bulk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On your list. Perhaps I should be more specific. Was it -- --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was not on the -- on the 92 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But it was on the spreadsheet in which you have the exhibits indicated you intend to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Registrar, could I ask again, then, for 65 ter 1334.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, the document now coming up on your screen is an order dated 30 October 1995 from General Gotovina to various units, including the 72nd Military Police Battalion as indicated at the end of the document. It begins that: "Due to the observed irregularities in the manner of reporting unusual events to the superior command by units and the violation of the chain of command in the command and control system, for instance, on 29 October 1995, when the duty officer of the 72nd Military Police Battalion first reported the fire in the military facility in Strmica to the COR at the Croatian army Main Staff rather than to the Split Military District operation centre, Knin forward command post ..." And then it goes on to order that the duty officer of a unit is obliged immediately to report by telephone any unusual incident and send an interim report within two hours, and so on. Now, Mr. Lausic, does this refer to the reporting -- to the daily reporting system that you referred to yesterday and that was reflected in the documents, the two documents we just looked at; or is the reference to the reporting of unusual events a reference to another form of reporting events that take place in the Split Military District?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have here is not reporting to a higher level in the structure of the military police. Rather, the duty officer of the 72nd MP Battalion reported of this event, that is, the fire, to the centre of operational command of the Main Staff rather than contacting the forward command post of the Military District of Split that was in Knin. He did not get in touch with the duty operations section of the administration. He contacted the Main Staff, that is to say, a level within the armed forces. The administration of the military police, as such, was part -- a part of the Ministry of Defence. It was a different line of reporting. He did not use the line of reporting inside the military police. What we are discussing here was the structured line of reporting that existed in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In this instance, the unusual event appears to be a fire. Would the occurrence of crimes, including looting and burning --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object, and I ask that the fire -- where the fire took place I think is going to be important, so if it's put to the witness, that it be put fully to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, as I read the preface to the order, the unusual event in question appears to be a fire in the military facility in Strmica, and my question was whether or not the occurrence of crimes by members of the HV would also be included as unusual events that would be reported?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object as to the vagueness of the question, Mr. President. Unusual events in what context? The witness has explained this is not a military police issue, and what regulation are we referring to, what reporting system, concerning what events?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. The objection is denied. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 72nd MP Battalion, much as any other unit within the Military District of Split, was duty-bound to report to the operations centre of the Military District of Split on any extraordinary events which took place in the unit. That was the vertical structure of reporting that was to be used, since one of the military units -- or, rather, since that military unit would be part of the Military District of Split. The duty office of the 72nd Battalion was supposed to report on all activities of the 72nd Battalion as a military police unit to more senior levels following the vertical structure of the military police. That is to say, they had to report to the military police administration in Zagreb. If one were to look for their reports of the duty office of the 72nd MP Battalion, in particular such reports for the 30th of October, 1995, that was sent to the duty office of the MP administration in Zagreb, probably, among other events or possibly in another chapter of the formatted report, we would also come across this particular event. The 72nd Battalion had two lines of reporting: towards the Split Military District and their operations centre and towards the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to round out that answer, Mr. Lausic, you said that the 72nd Military Police Battalion, much as any other unit within the Military District of Split, was duty-bound to report to the operations centre of the Military District of Split on any extraordinary events which took place in the unit; would crimes or the observation of crimes or the awareness of crimes be considered such an extraordinary event?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific? Do you understand by this the offences which took place within the establishment units of the 72nd Battalion, that is to say, their members - for example, if there were any cases in the 72nd Battalion of suicide, homicide, theft, or whatever - or does this concern the military policemen of the 72nd Battalion when exercising their duties in contact with other members of the Military District of Split? If a member of the 72nd Battalion committed suicide or if there was a homicide or theft, that would be an extraordinary event to be reported to the operations centre of the Military District of Split, using a special format of reporting and provided that it took place in the facilities where the battalion was billeted. Everything else would be covered in the regular type of reporting sent to the MP administration, and among other addressees, those reports went to the Split Military District as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, if I can have just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Lausic, if I could turn you back to your diary. That's P2166. And I'd like to direct your attention first to an entry of August 8th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's on page -- I'm not sure which references are most helpful to the registrar, but page 37 of the English and page 33 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And toward the bottom third of the page, we see the following entry: "The tasks of these reinforced patrols are, A, to arrest and/or destroy enemy groups and/or individuals on patrol directions; B, to prevent commission of crimes by HV members on patrol axes in case of interventions to hand over detained HV members to the local VP, military police unit." And an entry below: "0800 hours, General Cervenko - informed with the situation!" With an exclamation point.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, what was it that General Cervenko was informed of on that date?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to go back to the beginning of the document. My notes say that I got a call from Major Juric at 7.45. He was the officer in charge of the forward command post of the MP administration attached to the Military District of Split. He informed that the minister's order on the -- securing the storage depots was implemented. Then Brigadier Biskic specified that the depot was handed over to -- by the 72nd Company of the military police. He also reported on the tasks that are underway at that point in time. I can't recall exactly whether this was a short briefing with my deputy, whereupon I issued these tasks to him. I believe that is what happened. Yes, I think I was issuing those tasks to my deputy. These are the tasks I wanted to see implemented. In item 1, commanders, at the IZM of the 73rd, 72nd, then we have Major Juric, Major Cvitanovic, Colonel Kozic, they were to carry out all military police tasks in their zones of responsibility with the existing formations. I also ordered that the UVP reserve forces, that the 66 VVP be used to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I think you're reciting in some detail the -- all of the issues that are reflected in the diary entry, but my question was a bit more specific than that, and that is that the diary entry indicates that General Cervenko was informed of the situation, and, indeed, there is an exclamation point after that, which indicates, at least grammatically, that there was something significant about that, so I just wanted to ask you if you could recall the situation that General Cervenko was informed about.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is why I was reading, trying to see what was it that preceded this note that General Cervenko was informed of the situation. I was trying to jog my memory. I obviously acquainted him with the fact that the reserve forces, that is to say, the 66th Battalion was used to form ten groups as security for protected persons and delegations since some protected persons and ambassadors were going to the liberated territory. Then the three combat groups were formed with combat vehicles to go to the liberated territories in order to prevent crimes, et cetera, et cetera, and this is what the chief of the Main Staff was informed about, what the measures were undertaken by me, to improve the situation with law and order in the liberated areas, and to prevent crimes. This is it. I was reading the passages in order to jog my memory on what it was exactly that I informed General Cervenko of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to turn to another entry in the diary, but Ms. Henry Frijlink reminds me that I did not tender 65 ter 1334.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar, the number to be assigned to 1334 would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I'd like to direct your attention next to a diary entry a couple of days later for the 10th of August, 1995, and that's at page 39 of the English, page 35 of the Croatian. And specifically, Mr. Lausic, I'd like to direct your attention to an entry at the -- at the bottom of page 39 in English and also the bottom of the page in Croatian that's now on the screen. And that indicates that at 2100 hours, there was a telephone call from senior Lieutenant Matanic, commander of the 71st Military Police Battalion, and the entry indicates: "Informed that the commander of Gospic Military District, Staff Brigadier Mirko Norac, ordered the arrest of a larger group of members of one battalion of the 118th Brigade, a Home Guard Regiment, who refused to follow orders and go to the battlefield in the direction of Gornji Vakuf." Goes on to note that following consultations with Staff Brigadier Obradovic and personally with Staff Brigadier Norac, it was decided not to carry out the arrests but, instead, to let the tension die down. And I simply wanted to ask you if that was a reflection of one of the powers of the Military District Commander to order the military police to arrest members of the Croatian army who have committed or are suspected of committing a crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to object again. If he can cite the crime that has been committed there. I think we're talking about two different things here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was, for a moment, distracted because I had to sign five decisions. Therefore, I read the ... The objection is denied. The witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my diary, I noted down here that at 2100 hours, the commander of the 71st Battalion of the military police called me up and conveyed to me the order he had received from Staff Brigadier Mirko Norac who ordered the arrest of a large group of members of a battalion of the 118th Home Guard Regiment who had refused to go in the direction of Gornji Vakuf. So this was not a crime but, rather, a breach of military discipline, the refusal to follow orders. As a large number of members of the Home Guard Regiment were involved and there was a lot of tension, I contacted the operations centre of the Main Staff of the Croatian army with the then-duty officer of the operative centre, and that was Staff Brigadier Mate Obradovic. I also contacted Staff Brigadier Mirko Norac, who was the commander of the Gospic Military District, and it was decided that these persons should not be deprived of their liberty but that, rather, tensions should be alleviated because using a means of coercion would lead to trouble, but that, rather, the chain of command should be alerted so that there was no large-scale arrest of these soldiers. But this was not about a crime. It was about refusal to carry out orders. That's a breach of military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And let me explore that with you further. Had the occurrence in question been the commission of arson - the burning of houses, for example - would Brigadier Norac or any or Military District Commander have the power to order the military police to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, yesterday I believe there was reference to a couple of entries in your diary on the 13th and 15th concerning a top-level operational meeting. Let me first turn to an entry on the 11th, which was the first reference I saw to that impending meeting. That's on page 64 of the English, 58 of the Croatian. And just looking quickly at the entry under Mr. Moric's name, it indicates that on the 13th of September, 1995: "At 1000 hours in the Republic of Croatia MUP, top-level organisational meeting on the cooperation between MUP, military police, and Military District Commanders on the prevention of unlawful acts of torching, mining and looting in the newly liberated area." So I take it that was a reference to the anticipated meeting on the 13th, which was briefly discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Here, I say the assistant minister of the MUP; that means that we talked on the phone. Most probably, he rang me up, and these are bullet points as to what we agreed on, which was that on the 13th of September at 9.00 we would hold a top-level operational meeting on the cooperation between MUP, VP, and ZP commanders and the prevention of unlawful acts of torching, mining, and looting in the newly liberated area, that it was necessary for us to gather incoming data by zones of responsibility, and then that a joint inspection would be carried out at the highest level; I would go, my deputy, he with his assistants, Mr. Moric with his assistants, and through the chief of the Main Staff of the Republic of Croatia we would ask for approval to -- to participate and be engaged at a meeting of commanders of the following districts: Zabre [phoen], Karlovac, Gospic, and Split, and then a -- a summons arrived for the analysis of Operation Storm. What it says here, Brigadier Biskic, means that I informed Brigadier Biskic of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's turn to the -- your notes from September 13th at that meeting, then, and I wanted to look specifically at the comments by Mr. Moric at that meeting. And beginning at the third indicated paragraph, you indicate that Mr. Moric said: "We must implement measures that will guarantee implementation in the field of that which has been agreed upon on the higher level. "The line of command is not operational since on the level of the Military District they believe that they are either misinformed or that things are misrepresented or misinterpreted. We must make sure military commanders know the truth. "We must coordinate the activities of the military and civilian police, and the military commanders must know the truth and undertake preventative measures. "On 22 August 1995, it was decided that 'the line be drawn' and that we start with a new method of work. "We must find a way to have the civilian and military police work hand in hand." Mr. Lausic, can you tell us what Mr. Moric was referring to when he said: "The line of command was not operational since on the level of the Military District they believe they are either misinformed or that things are misrepresented or misinterpreted."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going object, Mr. President. For the record, the Prosecution had the opportunity to call Mr. Moric and decided not to, and to now ask this witness to speculate about what Mr. Moric meant I think is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that is a clearly improper objection at least in the context of an examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This objection should not have been made when the witness hears the objection. The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, if could you answer that question, please. Do you need me to ask that again?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question because I really didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, can you tell us what Mr. Moric was referring to when you said: "The line of command was not operational since on the level of the Military District they believe they are either misinformed or that things are misrepresented or misinterpreted."

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't answer that question. These are my bullet points, the notes I took while Mr. Moric was speaking. I took down his words faithfully, but at this time I really couldn't tell what you he meant, what he was thinking. I only noted down his words in his introductory remarks at the meeting we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me turn, then, to the military police coordination meeting that took place two days later on the 15th of September. And -- I'm sorry. I should have been clearer on that. That's the meeting at Plitvice, and it's a MUP military police coordination meeting as indicated by the heading. We talked about it briefly yesterday, and if I could turn to your comments on page 70 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that should be, Mr. Registrar, at the -- right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday about that first entry and about the structures, and you dealt with that yesterday. And then you say: "We must separate our personal from our professional stance when they differ in order to implement the proclaimed state policy." Can you explain to the Court what that was a reference to, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police, just like the civilian police, when carrying out its tasks in Operation Storm mobilised its reserve forces. I mobilised about 1500 reserve policemen, for example. I'm not sure what number the civilian police mobilised, but in any case, it was a large number of reserve policemen of the civilian police. The reserve forces of both the civilian and military police were local people from a certain area, and many of them had been expelled together with their families. They had been displaced and accommodated in temporary refugee centres. What I meant by what I said here was the following: Both members of the military and of the civilian police have to keep their emotions and frustrations under control. They have to subordinate them to their professional tasks. They must perform their professional tasks in such a manner that their attitude is strictly professional and that they should not be lenient towards members of the Croatian forces if they found them burning or looting. So what I said here was that we, the highest levels of leadership in the military and civilian police, had to convey this standpoint down the chain of command to the lowest-ranking policemen, both in the military and civilian police, whether active duty or reserve, and that they should be strictly told that their personal frustrations and emotions should not be confused with their professional work, that tolerating such crimes is detrimental to the state policy, that it creates an image which is harmful to the Republic of Croatia, and that they must be very energetic in carrying out their professional tasks. This is a brief explanation of what I meant when I said that we must separate our personal from our professional stance when they differ. I mean, for example, that if there is a reserve military police or civilian police at a check-point who had been displaced with his family and someone came along with stolen goods in their car, if such a person let that person pass through with stolen goods without taking any action, that would not be a good thing. Their emotions should not influence their performance of their professional tasks. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then your notes indicate, toward the bottom of the page: "Bring the line of command into the problem. Commanders at all levels must be aware of the problem and must resolve issues ... along the line of command [sic]." Now, with respect to commanders at the higher levels, with respect to Military District Commanders, did you consider the possibility of personally contacting those commanders, raising the problems with the line of command, and seeking their efforts in resolving it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have had an opportunity to present my daily reports, which were addressed along with Minister Susak to the highest-ranking military commander, the chief of the Main Staff, you will have seen that I describe the situation as it was in reality and propose what measures should be taken down the chain of command. It was to be expected that the chief of the Main Staff, based on my daily reports and also reports from other levels and services, should issue orders down the chain of command. My chain of reporting was the one you presented through my daily reports to the highest military and civilian structures. It was to be expected that the chief of the Main Staff, based on these reports, should respond down his chain of command and issue orders to lower-ranking officers, at lower levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what was intended, therefore, when your notes say "bring the line of command into the problem"? How was that intended to be accomplished?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the answer is contained in the attendees of that meeting at Plitvice who included the highest-level commanders, the commanders of battalions who were part of the Military Districts. These commanders of military police battalions, in their daily contacts, in their briefings, when they brief the commanders of the Military Districts or commanders at other levels, should insist -- they should insist that the chain of command should be used to prevent unacceptable behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, we turn then next --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, can we call up D567, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, D567 is a report by you dated 16 September 1995 regarding the analysis of the use of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia in Operation Storm, and it covers a number of areas. The first section indicates the planning and preparing of military police units in Operation Storm; the second section, the use of military police units in the preparation of Croatian army units for Operation Storm; section 3, the use of military police units at the beginning of assault operations and in liberating the occupied areas; section 3.4, under the subsection under that particular section at page 5 of the English and page 5 of the Croatian reflects the use of military police units to receive, escort, and process captured members of paramilitary units and the numbers of persons who were processed through 10 September 1995. It indicates, Mr. Lausic -- let me just ask you question about that. It indicates a total of 1576 persons escorted and processed from the beginning of Storm until 10 September 1995 and then the number of persons handed over to judicial bodies, so the number of persons escorted and processed being 1576. The number of persons handed over by the military police for whom there were reasons to suspect that they had committed criminal acts to the detriment of the Republic of Croatia was 659. Just for clarification, Mr. Lausic, that's -- that's a reference to Serbs suspected of activities against the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. These were members of the army of the so-called Sprksa Krajina, the army of the rebel Serbs on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We've seen a number of references in the documents and some of which you noted yesterday and I think referred to even the day before to the limited number of military policemen available, given the size of the territory and the events that were taking place. Can you give the Court any approximation of the number of personnel or percentage of personnel that was devoted to the task of processing the captured members of -- or suspected captured members of paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't be precise about that without seeing the analysis I prepared in 2004 when preparing for my interview with the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. In any case, they were employees of the crime detection military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we just turn quickly to a couple of other entries, and turning to page 8 of the English and page 9 of the Croatian. The heading in that section is: "Measures we undertook and continue to undertake to raise the general level of security in the newly liberated area of the Republic of Croatia. "By constant" -- it states that: "By constant visits to the newly liberated area of the Republic of Croatia, looking at the situation we found there an analysis of the state of security. We changed our tactics and methods of organising the military police and proposed to the HV Main Staff that they should take over the line of command to avoid disruption of public law and order, the commission of crimes, and in endangerment of traffic safety by members of the HV. These measures produced certain results but did not completely" -- well, the literal language here in English is "... did not completely the commission of prevent crimes ..." and I presume that's to mean did not completely prevent the commission of crimes, "... especially theft of property, torching houses, and individual acts of murder."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger said page 8. I believe he means page 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then finally, Mr. Lausic, just look down at the bottom of that page in English to the proposals you make. I think it's just after the -- in -- in English if we could raise that slightly and -- right. The first proposal is that: "The line of command should be assured by the presence of the HV Military District Commanders, officers responsible for security and information service, and political activity at working meetings which would be held in the coming period with assistance to the RH minister of the interior in all HV military districts who have areas of responsibility in the newly liberated territory, so that they take over responsibility for the conduct of members of the HV and lay down a line of command to control the movement of these soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so that the English is -- the English should be raised up to the first -- I guess that would be the previous page, then, if that's the case, and to the bottom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lausic, can you tell us what you intended by this proposal and the extent to which it was implemented after you made it -- or adopted and implemented after you made it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proposal was not implemented -- or, rather, meetings were not held at the level of the minister or assistant minister and myself as well as my deputy with the commanders of Military Districts. I don't know why that did not take place and for what reasons. I can merely say that those meetings were not held. At least, I made no note of them, and I don't seem to recollect any such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I could turn your attention back to page 9 of the English and page 8 of the Croatian. This is under a heading entitled: "The results of establishing military police duty in the newly liberated area of the Republic of Croatia." And it indicates that: "The military crime police, in collaboration with the Republic of Croatia MUP crime police, processed 321 crimes ..." And then it lists a number of crimes, including -- beginning with 13 murders, 18 cases of HV members dying accidentally, 191 cases of torching, 13 cases of setting explosive, 86 other crimes, chiefly theft. Of known perpetrators of the above crimes, 79 were HV members and 274 were civilians. As of the time of the report, September 16th, 1995, Mr. Lausic, were those 13 murders indicated at section 7 of the report the total number of alleged murders or possible murders that the military police had investigated?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not answer that precisely. This document entitled "analysis of the use of the military police" was compiled from reports sent by the heads of departments of the military police, the head of the crime service of the military police, the traffic military police, and other services, and they, in turn, received that information from their subordinate units. This is a compilation. Therefore, this part refers to the work of the crime police and, as such, was forwarded by the head of that department. It is merely as a point of reference in the document. Therefore, I cannot precisely answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not the military police was made aware of the number of civilian bodies or bodies determined to be civilians that were recovered or located after Operation Storm began?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the operation of sanitation units in the newly liberated territories that were collecting bodies?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not reported on those activities. Sanitation and hygiene measures within a given area is something that is undertaken pursuant to an order from the appropriate level. The military police was not duty-bound to be informed of that. Therefore, I did not have that information. I only know that commanders could issue orders on sanitation and hygiene measures to prevent outbreaks of disease, et cetera. In one of the numerous daily reports we have commented upon, I stipulated that sanitation and hygiene measures should be undertaken as soon as possible in the liberated area because there are -- there's dead cattle, roads are blocked, and all of those things can affect general security in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said you know that commanders can issue orders on sanitation and hygiene measures to prevent outbreaks of disease, and I -- do I assume correctly that's a reference in part to picking up both dead animals and dead human bodies to prevent the outbreak of disease?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I do not have a military background but a police one, I cannot tell you precisely what falls under the category of sanitation and hygiene measures. As a layperson, I would say that this would entail removing anything that can be dangerous to the health of people, and animals, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And were you informed at any time or did you receive information at any time that there was any investigation into the deaths of any of the persons whose bodies were picked up by sanitation units?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have such information. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Lausic, turning again to the proposals in your report, there are quite a number of proposals. Can you tell us what prompted in particular proposal number one, concerning the line of command, the proposal that you said was not adopted or implemented, or any of the other proposals?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please have that brought up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That begins at the bottom of page 10 of the English and page 9 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And actually, rather than having you read them all, let me ask to you focus on the first proposal that you said was not adopted. Can you tell us what prompted you to make that recommendation and proposal?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter part of the sentence is important, to take over responsibility for the conduct of members of the HV and lay down a line of command to control the movement of these soldiers, which means that, in practice, this was not the case. By virtue of the meetings that were to be held with the commanders, the need for them as the most senior commanders in their areas of responsibility, should lie down a chain of command by referring it to their subordinate command posts and to have the rules concerning the work and life of the members of the HV put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the Prosecution's examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before we have a break, Mr. Lausic, I would like to ask one or more additional questions. Could I take you back to the meeting that was held on the 13th of September in which Mr. Moric expressed that he was not satisfied with the attitude or approach of the military commanders and apparently expected them to undertake preventative measures. Now, did you form an opinion about whether such preventative measures should be undertaken by the military commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, completely right. Both Mr. Moric and I arrived at the same conclusions, and that is that the chain of command was needed to prevent the commission of crimes and that it needed to become more efficient or even operational because in some instances it simply did not exist. Perhaps I should explain. The commission of crimes was often caused but not disciplining HV members. Had the rules of the HV been followed, there would not have been as many crimes, and I can corroborate that by certain examples. For example, if a member, HV member steals a car and uses it for theft or robbery, that would have been prevented had the rules on the use of vehicles been followed, and that particular HV member would not have had the opportunity to steal the car and use it to commit crimes. The same model can be used when discussing the use of arms and other crimes. We wanted to ensure that commanders lie down the chain of command in order to have the rules of work and activities of HV members put in place, which to a large extent would prevent HV members to be in a situation in which they could potentially commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Moric said that the Military District level -- believed that they were misinformed or that things were misinterpreted. Did you form an opinion about that, as well, whether it was misinformation or -- so not knowing what actually was happening, or was it not wanting to know what actually was happening, or -- did you form an opinion about an explanation as to the attitude of the Military District level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally believe then, as I do now, that commanders at all levels, via the daily and interim reports they received from the military police as well as from their subordinate commanders, did have an opportunity to acquaint themselves with the situation in their respective areas. I can say another thing. There were also assistant commanders for security and information, that is to say, that person was in charge of security and was also duty-bound to report to the commander on all security-related events, much as the military police had to. They also had to report on the activities and behaviour of HV members within the commander's area of responsibility. That post is the assistant commander for security -- or, rather, for the SIS service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently at the meeting, Mr. Moric expressed some concerns in this respect. I hear from you that you had concerns in this respect as well. Did you share those concerns with Mr. Moric, either during or outside this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the meeting of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the meeting where Mr. Moric said that he -- that the activities of the military and civilian police should be coordinated and that military commanders must know the truth and undertake preventative measures. So my question was whether you, at this meeting or at any other occasion, you shared the concerns similar to the concerns Mr. Moric expressed with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Mr. President. I did not make separate notations of my own views expressed since this was my diary. I only noted down what Mr. Moric said. Reading the notes that refer to him, I agree fully with his views on the situation and measures to be undertaken, as well as the discrepancy between what was agreed upon and ordered and the situation in the field. This view of Mr. Moric's would be identical to my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question, however, is whether you shared, that you spoke about these concerns with him, either during this meeting or outside of this meeting, so that you told him what your concerns were and that he told you that he did or did not share your concerns.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Mr. President. At the meeting itself, I expressed my views which were identical to Mr. Moric's views, which I noted down. There was some discussion, and we all agreed on those views. We all agreed it to be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And where Mr. Moric said that military commanders must know the truth, did you form any opinion as to whether they knew the truth but didn't want to know it or that they really did not know the truth and should be informed about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same comment would apply to this situation as I said a moment ago. The commanders received reports from MP units, from their subordinate officers as well as their assistant commanders in charge of security, and by virtue of those, they had insight into the situation of their respective areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you ever speak about that with Mr. Moric, that you believed that they received information which would enable them to know the truth but that they apparently did not want to know it or did not understand it? Did you ever discuss this with Mr. Moric whether during this meeting or at any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to be precise since I have no verbatim notes of the meeting. In any case, we did discuss that, and I shared my views with him at that point in time, much as I did now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could make an objection either now or when we come back or -- outside the presence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll first give the witness the opportunity to follow the usher. We'll have a break, Mr. Lausic, for approximately 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Respectfully, I have to object to the leading nature of some of the questions that were posed. I just note for the record that on the transcript when the witness was asked on direct about this matter, he said he didn't know what was meant, and in the way the question was posed to him, it says: "Mr. Moric expressed that he was not satisfied with the attitude or approach of the military commanders and apparently expected them to undertake preventative measures..." is how you posed the question to him. I believe it was leading, and I think -- during cross-examination, I certainly plan to explore this topic, but for the record I feel compelled to note my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What I did, Mr. Misetic, is where you objected against the question put by Mr. Tieger, an objection which could easily be understood as an encouragement to follow your suggestion that whatever in addition to what we find on paper would be said by this witness as far as the remarks of Mr. Moric are concerned would be speculation. I asked some additional questions to explore where additional information would from a logical point of view not necessarily amount to speculation, whether there was any information known to this witness which would not be speculative and which would assist the Chamber in understanding the notes and the observations made by Mr. Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could just say briefly, Your Honour, to the extent you've now said it was encouragement. It is a perfectly legitimate objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I did not say it was encouragement. Would you please carefully listen to me: Could be understood as.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I said, nothing more, nothing less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if I could also add that it was an objection that is routinely made; the second point is, my objection was based on a prior ruling of the Chamber where you sustained the same objection with respect to Mr. Hjertnes, and that is the basis upon which I made the objection, just for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's on the record. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 25 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I take it you're the first one to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lausic. I would like to -- I wasn't planning on it, but I'd like to pick up where we left off at the end -- with the Presiding Judge's questions. If we could turn to Exhibit D567, Mr. Registrar, please. Mr. Lausic, what I'm pulling up on the screen is in fact your 16 September report to General Cervenko on Operation Storm. You will recall that the sequence of events that Mr. Tieger took you through this morning included some meetings with the MUP on the 10th, the 13th, and the 15th and some entries in that diary where one interpretation of the entry was put to you. I'd like to explore a different interpretation of what Mr. Moric was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could, Mr. Registrar, turn to page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a portion that Mr. Tieger didn't show you of this report. I'm going is show you a few documents, Mr. Lausic, because I don't want to spend a lot of time on this at the beginning, but if you would -- it's page 8 in the English, paragraph 6.3. And in describing the situation and how the military police was functioning, you wrote: "In larger villages and towns and along major roads, constant beat patrols ensured law and order, prevented torching and the uncontrolled removal of war booty, and controlled the safety of military road traffic." 6.4 says: "Non-stop traffic security was provided to HV units withdrawing from newly liberated areas. Security ensured for mobilisation assembly points where HV units were demobilizing, and public law and order maintained in places where official welcomes had been organised for HV units in towns all over the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could turn now to D1066.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the same day from the chief of the general military police, Mr. Kozic. You're familiar with Mr. Kozic, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You know --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Tell us who Mr. Kozic was on the 16th of September, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kozic, he was the chief of the general military police department in the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, here's his -- after the meeting at Plitvice -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm hearing questions before the translation is completed. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was listening to the French translation at that very time. Mr. Misetic, if you could try to adapt your speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is Mr. Kozic's report the day after the meeting in Plitvice. The chief of the sector for the general military police says: "According to our assessment, the security situation in the parts of the Republic of Croatia recently liberated in Operation Storm as to the area of responsibility of military police units and within the operation and assessment realm of the general military police is good and stable." That's on the 16th, Mr. Lausic. Now, if I can take you to what you wrote to General Cervenko on the 15th of August, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar - one moment, please - this would be Exhibit D292, please, on page 3. I'm sorry, it's ... page 13. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar. Paragraph 5.3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You wrote to General Cervenko: "In larger places and towns, 24-hour patrols and beat service are securing public peace and order, preventing arson and uncontrolled removal of the spoils of war, and taking care of road traffic safety; they are still securing major military depots in the liberated territory of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page, concerning conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the conclusion section, you wrote: "The preparation, planning, and engagement of military police units, the command of joint actions with the HV SIS, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Interior, were at a high level and the problems were solved as one went along. Therefore, we are of the opinion that units of the military police of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia performed all their tasks relating to the preparation and execution of the Operation Oluja." Now, my question to you, Mr. Lausic, is when Mr. Moric is saying that commanders think -- let me put my question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to say that if I did not have the original in front of me in the Croatian language what I hear through my headset as a Croatian interpretation of the extract read out by Mr. Misetic in English is completely different, so I find this distracting. I find it hard to focus because what I hear as an interpretation of what Mr. Misetic is saying differs from what I can see written down in the Croatian text, and I find this distracting and disconcerting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What we perhaps best do is that you read from the screen what this report exactly says because you will understand that if someone is sitting behind a desk translating word by word that the wording, the phrasing, might not be always be for the full 100 percent the same compared to a translation which still could be an accurate translation by interpreters who have to interpret immediately on the basis of the reading of Mr. Misetic. I further add to that, that the translation uploaded in e-court is a draft translation and not a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- confirmed translation. But perhaps if you read the original on your screen, that would certainly enable you to know exactly what Mr. Misetic is quoting. And I take it that those who speak and understand the language will verify whether there are any major mistakes in the draft translation. Can you read it, please? I think what Mr. Misetic read to you is found under the word "zakljucak" in the original, and apologies for my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Lausic, is, wasn't Mr. Moric really telling you that you in fact weren't conveying the gravity of the situation in reports such as this to the military commander?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to respond -- or, rather, comment on the report you presented, which was drawn up by Major Kozic and addressed to my deputy, Brigadier Biskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do it in a concise manner because we have much material, as you can see, to cover. But, yes, I will give you a chance to respond.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem. But I wanted to point out that the report you presented to me by the chief of the General military police, Major Kozic, is addressed to my deputy, Brigadier Biskic. And if you look closely at the material I signed as the analysis of the use of the military police, and if you look at the last page - that's page 11 in the original document - and if you look at the initials at the bottom left-hand corner, left -- left of the stamp and signature, it says MB/TH. These are the initials of Marijan Biskic/the typist who typed out the document, her initials, and from this one can conclude that it was my deputy who drafted this document, based on the report from the chief of the general traffic and crime military police department. I read it and signed it as the report of the military police administration, but I did not understand your question, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, first, regardless of who drafted it for you, I think you yesterday used the metaphor of commanders being in a relationship of parent and child. The persons that drafted were your metaphorical children, Mr. Lausic, and I'm putting it to you again, what Mr. Moric said at those meetings was that you - and by you, I mean the military police of which you were most responsible - were not accurately reporting to the military line about the gravity of the situation in the field. And if you disagree with me, I'll show you any of these three reports or the two that went to General Cervenko and ask where you say that the military police is unable to execute its duties because the line of command is not functioning.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with your opinion. I think the commanders were sufficiently informed of the realities on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You think that. But you agree that -- if they were informed of the realities, they weren't informed by you.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You saw from the reports addressed to the chief of the Main Staff and the other highest levels that this was my chain of reporting as the chief of the military police administration. Every day, they also received reports from the commanders of the military police battalions in their areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Believe me, we're going to get to all of those reports that you have referred to. What I'm interested in right now is the top of the chain. The top of chain, as you say, is you at the head of the military police administration and General Cervenko as the Chief of Staff, and in these reports, the written reports that you send to General Cervenko at the top of the chain, never once do you indicate that units are in the field burning and that the line of command needs to take action because the military police cannot handle the situation. Is that a fair statement about the content of these reports? And, believe me, as the days go by, we will go into the specific paragraphs of these reports. But, generally speaking, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, the chief of the Main Staff and all the other highest levels of command in the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff received a daily summary of security-related events, a daily bulletin issued by the duty service of the military police administration, and in this daily summary, there were segments dealing with the events that had taken place in the past 24 hours. These segments were crime, breaches of military discipline, traffic accidents, et cetera, et cetera. So the chief of the Main Staff and the other highest-ranking commanders in the Main Staff and in the Ministry of Defence were informed through the daily bulletin and had precise data as to when, where, how, by whom, all those seven questions that can be asked, all that was encompassed by those bulletins. My reports on the activities of the military police, the ones you are quoting now, were something special linked to that period. The bulletins covered the work and activities of the military police every 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, if I pause after you answer a question, it's not -- just so you are aware, it's -- I'm waiting for the translation, the interpretation to catch up. You need to -- it's not because I'm expecting you to continue with your answer, just so you're aware of that. Mr. Lausic, that's fine, and believe me, probably for tomorrow I'm going to print out all of those daily reports so that you have them in hard copy and you can review them. But based on those daily reports, I take it that we can conclude, based on the two general reports that you submitted, that those daily reports are not going to show us that the military police is unable to function or complete its tasks because if that were the case, you would have put that in your two reports; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, but as interpreted, your question was that the military police was incapable of carrying out its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No. Let me repeat the question. What I'm saying is, those daily reports are not going to show us that the military police was unable to complete its tasks because if that were true, you would have stated in your general reports to General Cervenko that, in fact, the military police was not able to complete all of its tasks; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports deal with the activities that the military police was carrying out. For the military police to be more successful in its activities, there would have been fewer events that they had to intervene in, if the lack of discipline among the soldiers of the Croatian army had been dealt with down their chain of command. To put it simply, we were doing as much as we could with the resources available to us, but we would have been more successful if the commanders down their chain of command made sure that the soldiers reported the rules of service, the rules of discipline, and other rules; and then we as the military police would have been more successful because we would have had fewer events to deal with in our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me wrap up this section for one minute. Mr. Lausic, it's always the case that there's always -- you can always do better. You can always have more discipline, even today. But in terms of the reports that you were sending to General Cervenko, do you agree with me that he never reported in those reports that there was anything extraordinary taking place on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at the reports day by day in order to give you a precise answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You feel free to do that if you have your book of documents. I'm referring you to the two reports which are your reports and analyses of Operation Storm. One is from the 15th of August; the other is with another month's time to reflect on it from the 16th of September. In those two reports, do you agree with me that you didn't report that there was an extraordinary situation taking place on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see that on the screen, please, because I can't find them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the interest of time, Mr. Lausic, I think you have them in your binder. If you want to let me know after the next break if you have found anything in those reports which would say there was something extraordinary, I'd be happy to let do you it. But it will take us a bit of time it flip through all of the pages on the screen. Mr. Lausic, let me change topics for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 478 on the screen, please. I'm sorry. That is now, for the record, Exhibit P2189.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I'd ask to you take a look at this. This is your order of the 6th of October, 1995, and the Chamber is aware of a killing incident in the village of Varivoda as well as several other killings incidents that took place after Operation Storm, and if you take a look at this order, you issued an order to create an operative action, and you named it Varivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page in the English, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of the document, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I just wanted to clarify something so there won't be any confusion. I think there may be a misunderstanding that all -- about whether or not all of the documents that were on the Prosecution's exhibit list were in Mr. Lausic's binder. I think he only had a -- some of those documents. So it shouldn't be an assumption that all of the documents on the exhibit list are available to him in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. If I could just -- in order -- because Mr. Lausic seems to be flipping through his binder looking for documents. If the OTP could give us what he was given, and then I can instruct him whether a document is in his binder or not. I think it'll speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if I have that handy, but I'll try to get it as quick as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, Mr. Tieger advises us that it's in fact not in your binder, so you'll have to look at the screen in front of you. Now, can you take a look at this. You wrote and, actually, on the cover page you addressed it to the 72nd Rijeka Military Police Battalion - the 71st, I'm sorry - the 72nd Split MP Battalion, and the chiefs of MP administration sectors. And in the preamble, you say: "Through an analysis of the security situation ... we have come to the conclusion that the security situation is not at the required level, and in order to raise the general state of security, ... in cooperation with the MUP, I am establishing operative action Varivoda." And then it says how long the action will be in effect. In paragraph 1, you name the officers who will be in the commission, including three officers from the military police administration. You appoint the commanders of the -- I believe it's the 3rd Company of the 72nd MP Battalion and 4th Company of the 72nd Zadar Battalion and the commander of the company of the 72nd Knin MP Battalion. At point 2, you order them to cooperate with the chiefs of the police administrations in the area, perform an analysis -- "... on the ground, shall perform an analysis of the security situation of the work organisation to date, and draft an operative plan for the use of the military police and the police in the implementation of operative action Varivoda." You then identify what -- how long the shifts are going to be. In paragraph 4, you tell them to use search dogs. Paragraph 5, you say: "The commander of the operative action Varivoda team is authorised to take all measures in order to have the level of responsibility and performance quality of military and police tasks raised to the highest level. The commander is also authorised to agree on the tactical and methodological implementation of the operative action with representatives of the RH MUP." Point 6, you order that reports be sent through the operations duty of the MP administration and a summary report at a meeting in the MUP administration on the 11th of October. You see who it's addressed to: the Minister of Defence, Assistant Minister Rebic, and Mr. Moric. Now my first question -- let me wait. What Article of the rules of the military police allowed you to issue this order?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 8 of the rules on structure and work of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your order. You're getting involved in how long the shifts are going to be, the use of dogs, how the reporting is going to go. You're getting involved in operational matters in this case. What rule of the rules of the military police allowed to get involved in operational matters? And I also say that you then empowered the team leader to draft the operative plan, the team leader being Mr. Kozic, who, again, is from the MP administration in Zagreb. Where did you get the power to issue those orders and get involved in operational matters?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we go back to the beginning of the order, you see that it refers to two MP units and three departments of the MP administration, that is to say, to different organs within the structure. The order has to do with a clearly defined action. The headquarters is determined, as well as the tasks, means, tactics and methodology in the course of the action as well as the way of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is an operation much like this exact same thing that happened in Operation Storm; right, Mr. Lausic? You did the same thing prior to Operation Storm. You sent down people from Zagreb, set up your IZM, issued orders on what was to be done, how the reporting was going to go; right? This is Operative Action Varivoda; that was Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not equate the two orders, the preparatory order for the implementation of military police tasks in the course of Operation Storm and the order on the establishment of Operative Action Varivoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My initial question, Mr. Lausic, and let me get back to that, is what rule of the military police rules allowed you to issue this order for OA Varivoda?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered. It is Article 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And -- you're right, and my next question was -- let me put it a different way. Article 8, then, also allowed you to get involved in how the operation was going to be conducted; right? The methods, the tactics, the reporting system, who was going to be involved, how many men, all of those things you were allowed to do under Article 8; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that the military police with its equipment, staff, resources and the best possible methods and tactics be as efficient as possible. That is the strategic level of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, there's also an operational level of command and control, and if in fact this operation started to unfold in a manner that was inefficient or that wasn't producing results, you had the power to issue an additional order to fix whatever eventual problem would come up; right?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is it what was done. By changing the methods and tactics of the activities of the military police, by reinforcing or strengthening certain parts or units of the military police, it was done continually, as can be seen from all the documents that have been presented in the course of the past two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lausic, let me turn your attention to your statement, which is P2159. And at paragraph 19, you talk about the passage of the temporary instructions. You say in the middle: "We gave general instructions referring to the organisation of the military police, the speciality of the military police, the setting-up of commanders in the military police, thus regulating the vertical subordination in the military police and the horizontal coordination of the work of the military police." Did you find that in your statement, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number of the paragraph in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. This is in your statement where you talk about the concepts of vertical subordination and horizontal coordination, and let me show you before I ask you a question on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 1D66-0243.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm going to show you, Mr. Lausic, you probably don't have in your binder, so you will have to look on the screen is your annual report on the work of the military police for 1994, and we have an excerpt translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 1 in the English, please, which is, fortunately, page 1 in the Croatian. It's numbered page 1, I apologise, which is page 3 in the English, and numbered page 1 in the Croatian version, which is page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
