utterances.text: Now, in this section you talk about the work that was done in 1994 with the military police, and this is now after the passage of the 1994 rules, and you say, at paragraph 3 -- this is the section, by the way, titled: "General features of the structure, development, and the work of the OS RH military police in 1994."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You wrote: "The results, the level of organisation, and development of the military police until the end of 1993 were the subject of analysis on the MP administration level and the basis for determining the focal tasks in the development of the military police in 1994 as following." In point 3, there is: "Strengthen and building the system of command and control according to a vertical subordination and an operational daily system of control according to a horizontal coordination." Now, Mr. Lausic, explain to us the concept of vertical subordination and daily operational horizontal coordination.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question you have put is something that was quite troublesome for all the commanders during the years I headed the military police, of which seven were the war years. These rules from 1994 were in force until 2004. This question basically arose from the lack of wish to fully comprehend what is vertical command and control and horizontal coordination. That lack of understanding existed while the interim instructions were in place that were put into force in January 1992. For that particular reason, the military council of the Ministry of Defence had to sit and the Minister of Defence personally had to explain the two concepts. May I conclude my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will let you conclude, but if you would first just specifically tell me what it means, and then if it's necessary to go into the background, I don't have a problem with it. But if you could first tell us, what does it mean when you say vertical subordination and daily operational horizontal coordination. How does that system work?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained that in the course of the first day of my testimony when answering one of Mr. Prosecutor's questions, when stating what were the tasks of the MP administration as well as my authority under Article 8, and Article 9 envisaged the right to implement daily operational tasks in everyday activities to the various commanders of the armed forces in Croatia. I may repeat that, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't want you to repeat anything that you already said. What I am interested in is, up until now, you have used the phrase that the 72nd MP would report according to their two verticalities, yet in 1994 you explained the concept as really one verticality and one horizontal coordination. In fact, that's the way we should look at it structurally, is that the MP battalion is coordinating its work under Article 9 but is subordinated under the command and control of the chief of the military police administration.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When performing regular military policing tasks, the Military District Commander within whose establishment that unit is. The military police battalion active in the given area of the Military District daily received dozens of specific orders at various command levels within the Military District. Such orders had to do with escorting military convoys, requests to provide security, or other tasks that were within the remit of work of the military police. That included daily operational command of MP units in accordance with Article 9 and its implementation. From the archives of the MP battalions as well as the administration archives, I could show you thousands upon thousands of such orders sent by all-level commanders, brigade commanders, Military District Commanders, thus exercising their powers from Article 9 in terms of daily operational command of MP units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to get behind what that means, Mr. Lausic, and I'd like to show you via Sanction --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, a witness statement given to the OTP and which obviously we will not be tendering into evidence, so I haven't uploaded it into e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the statement given by Petar Stipetic who, as you know, was -- took over command up in Sector North during Operation Storm, and you referred to General Stipetic in your statement as a professor type. You corrected that to say you didn't mean he was literally a professor but that based on his knowledge, he was a professorial type of general. And if we could turn the page in Croatian and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been out of the courtroom for a while, so I'm not I recall the precise protocol for using statements of perhaps-anticipated witnesses, but it's certainly not a practice I'm accustomed to in my jurisdiction, and I thought at a minimum there was an effort to elicit answers from the witness generally -- and the bottom line, of course, is now the statement clearly won't come in. I'm not sure what the purpose of using it now before a highly specific question to which this -- to which an answer has been obtained and for which the basic proposition for which this might be a good-faith basis is at issue. Otherwise, we've got all kinds of -- it's one thing to put your case to a witness. It's another thing to advance propositions generally through statements that should properly be advanced through witnesses who are going to be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the guidance of the Chamber was that you first asked the witness questions about a certain matter, and if there is any need to then put to him that others may have given the same answers or different answers, that you do that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do not -- of course, the Chamber doesn't know the statement, and the Chamber doesn't know what you'll ask the witness about in relation to the statement. Therefore, whether it has been properly dealt with first without the statement, the Chamber wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, the guidance may be clear. If the previous questions were very much about concepts of subordination and coordination, if that is what this statement relates to, then it can be put to the witness. If not, then, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We've been here ten months. Every time we pull a statement up, we get an objection that we have to go through the procedure. By this point, I have been trained very well to know that we have to go through the hoops. So based on the witness's last answer about what types of daily orders they would give, it's on the transcript, and that's the exact issue that I would like to put. In addition, the concept of daily operational control I think for three days now has been talked about extensively. So there's no risk of a new matter being put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first wait for your question and what portion to be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, and I take it that you will be very attentive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this was the question. Another unit was a military police battalion. Were those battalions subordinated to the military police sector in the Main Staff or to the Ministry of Defence? You can read it on your screen, Mr. Lausic, and I'll skip over some of this, but he says: "In the beginning, the military police battalions were under the command of the Main Staff. One military police battalion was directly under the Main Staff. Such standing has lasted only for two to three months. Then President Tudjman decided that the administration of military police must be established in the Ministry of Defence. Those MP battalions which were under the command of the Main Staff before from then on fell under the command of the Ministry of Defence. MP battalions in the operative zones ..." which is another term for Military Districts, "... stayed within the zones but because of the new centralised command system, they were responsible to the military police administration in the Ministry of Defence regardless that they are in the operational zone. Whenever the commander of the operative zone needed military police, he had to inform the military police administration in the Ministry of Defence." There's another question about clarifying about giving orders, a Military District Commander giving orders to a battalion commander, and General Stipetic said: "It should be normal for a Military District Commander to give orders to a military police battalion commander, but before giving such orders he would have to consult with the military police administration. Independently, he can give minor tasks: Control of traffic, dealing with drunk soldiers, providing security to transportation of some equipment, et cetera. But larger engagement of the military police had to be approved by the military police administration, and it's for the chief of the military police administration of the Ministry of Defence to decide whether to give additional forces to a Military District command [sic]." Now, Mr. Lausic, that in fact is an accurate statement of how things worked under the new system that you, in fact, were the proponent of, which was that this concept of horizontal coordination meant that the district commanders could use the military police for their purposes to execute their tasks, but vertically the MP battalions were subordinated to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. My only concern is this. Happy to have the witness direct his attention to the document. I'm just concerned about a question that seems simultaneously to ask about the accuracy of the document and about this witness's positions about aspects of subordination and coordination. So if those could be separated, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you split them up, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, the Military District Commander as a daily operational command can issue orders to the MP battalions as you said by the dozens, perhaps, for minor tasks like control of traffic, dealing with drunk soldiers, providing security to transportation. But he couldn't deploy the military police battalions throughout a significantly large amount of territory without your approval; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely incorrect. Completely incorrect. The problem of vertical subordination and horizontal coordination, first of all, met with certain commanders who had originated from the Yugoslav People's Army where the system of coordination and command was set up completely differently with different tasks. You should have asked that. General Stipetic, I was not a JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What you're familiar with --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It's actually an important point. You are familiar with how the military police was structured?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- the witness is answering the question, attempting to get through the question. Then he's stopped and turned to a different question. I think he should be permitted to answer his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I want the answer to the original question, but while he's on this point -- I think he knows and this is precisely the point, and if necessary I'll take him to a document to that effect --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But the difference between the JNA system and the system you implement.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would allow me to finish first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question was very short. "Correct?" The answer was it is completely incorrect. If you put a question in this way to the witness, he may answer the question, and especially if he asks to be allowed to continue, then to say: "Sorry. It is actually an important point ..." and then put a different question to the witness is not appropriate. You may finish your answer, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Mr. President. Immediately after the interim instructions on the work of the military police was put in place in January 1992, certain commanders of the HV attempted to behave in opportunistic manner so as to use the newly -- the existing system of command and control. For that reason, the minister of defence in December 1992 held a meeting of the military council. In attendance were the chief of the Main Staff, General Tus, then all the other most senior officials. It was at that meeting that command and control was discussed, in terms of the military police. It was an item on the agenda of that meeting of the military council. That happened because there was a misunderstanding on the part of the commanders of the new system of command and control of the military police. At the meeting of the military council -- I will be brief. I will respond in a single sentence, if I may, Mr. Misetic. At the meeting, it was precisely determined what were the tasks of the MP administration, which commands and controls all MP units through the following items which I have specified in the course of the first days -- day of my testimony. What follows in the text is that the HV unit commanders or garrison commanders within whose area of responsibility the specific MP unit is command MP units to execute all military policing tasks in keeping the authority and powers of work of the military police. They're also tasked with daily monitoring of the work of the MP and notify the MP administration with the proposal of measures to be undertaken by the administration so as to ensure efficient functioning of the MP unit. Immediately after --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, that's more than one sentence. I'm trying to make some progress here, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put a very serious question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have additional documents that --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I want to provide a serious answer. After the interim --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, we have to keep in mind that if we speak at the same time, it will not be put on the record. If we speak too quickly, that the interpreters have no possibility to translate, and if you tell us that you'll be brief and respond in a single sentence where many do follow, then that is a reason to invite you to focus your answers very much on the precise question. Perhaps during the break, the witness can think this over, and as far as simultaneous speaking, you could do, as well, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I show him one document before the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that would give us a more appropriate moment for the break, then, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let me show you 1D66-0260. 1D66-0277. This is from the 4th of July, 1995. It's your response to some -- to an analysis by General Stipetic, and you took particular exception to the portion where he analysed the structure of the military police, and apparently in that document, General Stipetic -- you write: "... once more brought to the attention the question of command and control over the military police by stating the following ..." And then General Stipetic wrote -- at point 2, he suggested that. "The brigades and Home Guard Regiments should within their composition have a military police platoon or, rather, to incorporate military police platoons within the brigades and Home Guard Regiments which would be placed under their direct command." He additionally wrote: "The current command and control system of the military police is not effective and hinders the possibility of a more rapid engagement of the military police because it requires the use of long indirect routes." You responded: "We feel that the remarks stated by Colonel General Petar Stipetic are arbitrary and have no factual basis, and the grounds for our opinion are as follows ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You wrote towards the middle of that page: "I would also like to emphasise that military police units have until now and will in the future carry out all of their tasks in a planned manner in the areas of combat activity according to the plans of the 'engagement of military police units in their areas of responsibility upon the commencement of actions by HV units.' The stated plans are coordinated with the headings of the engagement of HV units and were created in cooperation with the HV Military District Commands." You then write in the next sentence: "Regarding the proposal that military police platoons should be incorporated at HV Brigades and Home Guard Regiments and placed directly under the command and control of the commanders of the HV Brigades and Home Guard Regiments, we had this type of structure until the beginning of 1993." And then you talk about how that was -- another system of command and control was accepted: "In 1993 and 1994, there was a restructuring conducted." Now, it seems to me that the dispute there between you and General Stipetic is General Stipetic wants military police units to be under the direct command of military commanders, and you disagreed with that. Is that an accurate representation of what this dispute was about?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. The organisation of the military police --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, then, a more specific question. What type of system was General Stipetic advocating, and why did you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question requires us to go back into the past, time permitting and by His Honour's leave. But briefly, I can say it's contained in the first several points of my testimony, both in my suspect interview and the transcript and in my witness testimony. When the military police units in the first few days, when the Croatian army was being created, were led directly by the brigade commanders, the Crisis Staffs and all those who established some sort of military police and many abuses of the military police or misuses were registered. Military policemen were carrying out tasks not following within the purview of the military police, and for this within the president of the Republic as the commander in chief issued a decision on a different organisation of the military police and established the military police administration before I was appointed to that duty. In the sector of security and intelligence of the Ministry of Defence, the military police administration was established before I took up my duty as its chief. It was only after my appointment that I set out to do the work I have already described. This organisation was never approved, nor does it exist today. Now, a regiment of the military police --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this again. What did General Stipetic want?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted the same model that existed in the former JNA, for every brigade to have a military police unit under the direct command of that brigades commander who would be the only one receiving reports. That was the situation we had in 1991 and 1992 in the war, and there were some abuses. The flow of information was stopped. We had local sheriffs, local power-holders, maybe brigade commanders and so on, and this system was never implemented, although there was constant pressure to have it restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Last question before the break, Mr. Lausic. What does General Stipetic -- what do you understand him to mean when he says that the current command system is not effective because it hinders the possibility of more rapid engagement because it requires the use of long, indirect routes? What does he mean -- what is the route that he is talking about there as being a long, indirect route?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should have asked him that. I'll tell you that with all the commanders, first, of the operative zones while they existed and then with all the commanders of a Military District, including your client, General Gotovina, as soon as he took up his duties as the commander of the Split Military District, I and my deputy held talks with them, at which we directly explained the command and control structure of the military police, and we always ended each such meeting by me saying, Sir, whatever falls within the purview of the military police has to be carried out by the unit which is part of your Military District, or operative zone. As soon as a battalion commander tells me he has been given a task which he cannot implement for whatever reason, lack of resources or whatever, these resources, vehicles, reinforcements will be provided by me, but the task has to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll get into some of those decisions that you made either accepting or rejecting General Gotovina's requests for military police maybe tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D66-0277 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections by Mr. Tieger. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1279.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness already be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the temperature in this courtroom is concerned, I'm usually not relying on Wikipedia, but I learned that a sigh is an exhalation of air through stress, boredom, relief, tiredness, longing, contentment, exasperation or disappointment. This Chamber sometimes has difficulties in perfectly interpreting what kind of sigh we hear, and there is, although I'm not referring to the context in which those words are used, but Shakespeare, at least, used the phrase: "A thousand thousand sighs to save..." We'll have a break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, could we please have on the screen 1D66-0262, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, I'm going to show you an order of yours from the 3rd of December, 1994. This is the order where you establish the areas of responsibility for the military police units, and you've addressed it to all of the military police units. And then if we could turn the page, please. I'm interested in paragraph 7. It talks about the various units, but obviously we're most concerned here with the 72nd Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we could go to numbered paragraph 7 in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you write that the: "... 72nd MP Battalion carries out military police tasks in the area of responsibility of the Split Military District and the southern front. "The commander of the 72nd MP Battalion is subordinated in daily operational commanding to the commander of the Split Military District. "Platoon and company commanders outside of the headquarters of the 72nd MP Battalion command are subordinated in daily operational commanding to the HV garrison commanders or the most senior HV commander within their area of responsibility." And then you have subordination of the 6th company to the commander of the southern front. Now, I'm trying to understand this structure, Mr. Lausic. It seems that have you taken the commander of the 72nd MP Battalion and subordinated him to the commander of the Split Military District, and then the company and platoon commanders that are not in the headquarters of the 72nd MP Battalion are subordinated to different commanders in daily operational commanding, including the garrison commanders or the most senior HV commander, within their area of responsibility. Can you explain the multiple subordination of the units that comprise the 72nd MP Battalion? I should say multiple daily operational subordination.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you are using the correct term. The units of the military police or, rather, the military police of the Croatian army was organised along the territorial principle. The logic was where the army is, there is also military police there. The 72nd MP Battalion whose headquarters was in Split had a company in Split. It had its command, a general police company, and a traffic company. There was one company in Zadar, one in Sibenik, and I don't remember where the 5th Company was -- oh, yes, it was in Sinj, and the 6th Company was in Dubrovnik. As the southern front existed at the time, which extended from Ploce to Dubrovnik, and had its commander, the 6th Company in carrying out its daily operational tasks was subordinated to the commander of the southern front. That was the so-called territorial organisation, which is not unknown in the world. The German military police is still organised along the same lines. We did not simply copy foreign organisation but simply responding to the needs that we had in view of the time and the territory. We organised this according to the logic of wherever the army is there, the military police is also. The companies had dislocated platoons. I'm not sure where the 72nd had those platoons, but I know that some platoons were dislocated in some battalions. If a company commander in Zadar received an order from the commander of the Croatian army brigade in Zadar to carry out a military police task, and to carry out that task he had insufficient equipment, men, resources, vehicles, and so on, and the task fell within the purview of the military police, he would apply to the commander of the 72nd Battalion, asking for help, and he would be provided with the requisite men, vehicles, and so on, and the task had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. This -- that at the end is what I went to get into. You said: "The company commander in Zadar receives an order from the Croatian army brigade in Zadar." Does that mean that, under the order that's on the screen, that the company commander in Zadar was subordinated for daily operational purposes to the commander of the Croatian army brigade in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend on who the most senior officer was. If Zadar had a Military District Commander, or as we know from the instructions we saw yesterday on the establishment of Military Districts, they could be appointed by name, or it could just be the most senior officer in the area. In any case, that would give the right to the most senior officer in Belgrade [as interpreted] to use his right to command the military police as described in Article 9 of the Rules of Service of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the city referred to there was Beograd. It was translated as Belgrade, which may cause some confusion in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to Beograd rather than to Belgrade, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Beograd and not Belgrade, correct, Mr. Lausic?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned neither Belgrade nor Beograd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll read the line: "In any case that would give the right to the most senior officer in ..." and where did you locate this most senior officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zadar, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In Zadar, "... to use his right to command the military police as described ..." It's now on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, structurally speaking -- and we've heard some expert testimony here about the need and the principle of unity of command. Now, if -- let's take as a hypothetical that the highest-ranking commander in Zadar is the commander of the brigade. The company of the military police in Zadar, then, the commander of that company, would have been subordinated for daily operational purposes to the commander of the brigade in Zadar; but what I don't understand is there would appear to me to be multiple lines of command here because the company commander is also answerable to the 72nd MP Battalion commander. The brigade commander has his own line of command that would go to the Split Military District. There's another line that goes to you in the police administration. Now, if -- who is commanding -- there's a lot of commanders here that seem -- if it's as if you say, there are a lot of commanders here who seem to be able to all issue their own orders to the military police company commander in Zadar, and if you could explain that, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple. The purpose and aim of such an organisation and the basic reasons for Article 8 and 9 are the following: Everything that falls within the purview of the military police has to be carried out, and there must be no delay in carrying out the task because there is a lack of men, resources, vehicles, and so on. Secondly, abuses in the use of the military police have to be prevented. The military police must not be used for purposes not falling within the purview of the military police as had happened in the first wartime years, and this is actually what prompted the changes in the previous organisation, when a platoon commander, for example, who was a member of a brigade, was responsible only to the brigade commander, carrying out whatever he was ordered to do regardless of whether it fell within the purview of the military police or not, and let me remind you that today in Croatia there are many trials where the accused are members of such units who did things they shouldn't have done. Secondly, the report on the fact that a commander in Zadar had carried out a task on orders from the commander of a certain unit - in this case, the brigade which was in Zadar - would reach the commander of the 72nd Battalion, and the battalion commander would know what the company commander had done, whether these tasks fell within the purview of the military police, whether he had had any problems with lack of men, resources, equipment, and so on or not. So everything that fell within the purview of the military police had to be carried out; secondly, there should no misuse of the military police; it should not be made to do things which do not fall within their job description; and, finally, the tasks -- everything had to be reported up the military police hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, isn't one of the benefits to the system that was put in place in 1994 the fact that there was now an architecture put in place, a system where there was centralised means of being able to issue orders to the various military police battalions, companies, platoons, in order have some consistency in coordination in terms of what the different companies and platoons would do in a given situation?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By whom? The battalion commander? When commanding the companies that were part of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's take Operation Storm as an example. Operation Storm involved the liberation of territories that crossed the boundaries of the Split Military District, went to the Gospic Military District, the Zagreb Military District, the Karlovac Military District, but if you wanted to have the military police all operating consistently across those Military Districts, who is the person that can achieve that? Having one plan all-coordinating, how can that be affected?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must confess that this is a very unclear question. It was all defined precisely in the order on the preparation of forces of the military police for Operation Storm, the so-called preparatory order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And who issued the preparatory order?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was presented here yesterday or the day before, and you could see that I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if could I tender 1D66-0262, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no objection in principle. However, it's a partial translation. I, you know, presume that the untranslated portions don't have any relevance to the issues raised here, but I think we need an opportunity to look it over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll do that by court tomorrow, I think. We'll look it over quickly, and if there's any -- if Defence can assist if they have any -- if they know specifically what those previous items in the order are and can illuminate, that would help as well. It doesn't have to be now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can just tell him. There are just for the different military police battalions across Croatia, who they're subordinated to. I didn't think it was relevant to this case, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I don't doubt that. Just a matter of due diligence. We'll look it over. We'll respond tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's be practical. We decide already on admission because there is no objection, but there's an opportunity for the Prosecution to ask the Chamber to revisit the matter. Would that be a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because we have no real objection. Mr. Registrar, that would be number ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1280 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm also reminded that I failed to tender 1D66-0262, which is the annual report prepared by Mr. Lausic for 1994 of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's also a partial translation. I don't know if they also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I gave the wrong number. 1D66-0243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that'll become Exhibit D1281.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1281 is admitted into evidence with the same proviso as with the previously document. Mr. Tieger, since we're doing bookkeeping anyhow, earlier today you said that 65 ter 3343 was on the Excel sheet. I had difficulties in finding it, but there was no objection from the Defence. It was not on your 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- ter list, you said, but it was on the Excel sheet, you said, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the oversight. I'm grateful it came into evidence. I will simply say that the representation that was on the sheet was based on -- was actually based on checking beforehand. I guess the information I received was wrong, but it wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You get some message at this moment, so perhaps it's better ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I can -- the message I get at the moment is that at least at a minimum, it was provided to the Defence by e-mail before Court. As far as being on the Excel sheet, I may have been wrong about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. But there were no objections, so there's no need to decide on the matter. It's just, again, that the Chamber encourages the parties to be as precise as possible in whatever information they give to the Chamber. Please proceed, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, if I could take you to Exhibit D267, please. This is the 2nd of August order you prepared and issued to the military police battalions. If I could take you to, first, paragraph 10 of this document, and you were shown this yesterday. Concerning Mr. Juric, it says you appointed Mr. Juric and a group of officers from the regular VP section and the VP crime section to assist in commanding and organising the activities. And then in the last sentence there in the middle paragraph: "The commanders of the 72nd VP Battalion and 73rd VP Battalion shall be subordinated to Major Ivan Juric." If we go to paragraph 12, please. This was, again, a discussion about the reporting system: "Within the daily operational chain of command ... it shall be subordinated for the commanders of the military police" -- sorry. "... the commanders of military police battalions ... shall be subordinated to the commanders of Military Districts ..." And then if we can turn the page in English. You order that the commanders of the 72nd VP Battalion and 73rd VP Battalion are to submit their reports to Major Juric who shall report to the VP administration. My first question is, Mr. Lausic: Why weren't the daily reports enough? Why did you issue an order for reports from those officers that you sent in the field to first be sent by the battalion commanders to your officers and then to you rather than to the Military District Commander? Why not just rely on the daily reports?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is regular practice in all police forces of the world applied to the military police of the Republic of Croatia that I organised, and that entailed that each every operative action, whether it be a combat operation as was this case, or be it an operative action such as the one in Varivoda where the focus was to improve the situation with law and order and crime in a given area, or whether it concerns providing security to an official, such as the President of the Republic or some other action. Once the tasks in the course of the action had been undertaken, as regulated by orders, reporting is also mentioned on the completion of tasks. But this does not go against a system of daily reporting on the completion of all tasks that fall within the scope of authority of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you also, then, tell Major Juric, Send a copy to me but you should be sending your reports to General Gotovina, let's say? It's an operative action. The reporting by your officer in the field according to the order goes to you. You don't even say, And copy the Split Military District Command. What would --

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need. Major Juric, much as Major Cvitanovic and Colonel Kozic, all of whom were at forward command posts as I've explained yesterday, it is they that I delegated part of my authorities to them based on Article 8. They were my eyes and ears in the field, so to say, in the course of the action. Major Juric received reports from the commander of the 72nd and the 73rd Battalion and then sent a compiled report to me. The commanders of those units forwarded their respective orders to their Military District Commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Why different reports? Why weren't you satisfied to just receive a copy of the daily operational reporting that was going to the Split Military District? In other words, I don't understand why either you didn't just rely on the same report that would go in the regular daily report or, alternatively, with this extra report that you ordered to be prepared by 8.00 every night, that you didn't say, And this second report should also be copied to the Military District Commander. Why are there different reports?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military District Commander receives reports from the commanders of the brigades, which are within his AOR. The commander of the forward command post of the MP administration, in this case, Major Juric, compiled reports that came from the 72nd, 73rd Battalion commanders plus their own -- or his own remarks. He was my forward command post commander. He was my eyes and ears in the field. I wanted to hear from him whether there were any problems in implementing tasks, in the functioning of command, whether he needed additional forces and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to paragraph 5, if we can, in this order. Now at paragraph 5, you talked about how you're at the strategic level. Let's talk about the operational level. You write: "A plan of unit's engagement at the start of combat operations shall be worked out in detail on the level of the VP battalions, companies, and platoons in all areas of responsibility, which will include setting up strong check-points with the task of preventing [sic] unauthorised and uncontrolled entrances [sic] into the zones of combat operations ..." If we go to paragraph 6, the second sentence. You go further, and you say -- and you refer to an order that was issued on the 1st of May, 1995, and you say: "The tasks under item 2.2 shall be only performed at large cross-roads for the purpose of directing traffic in the area, and after the HV members reach certain lines and take defensive positions, strong check-points shall be set up at the access and exit roads of the defence zone without the presence of RH MUP members. It shall be ensured" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: "It shall be ensured that the military police members take vigorous actions and perform the tasks in accordance with the authority of the armed forces military police." Why does paragraph 5 put it on the level of the VP battalions, companies, and platoons to work out their plan of engagement rather than the commanders to whom they are operationally -- daily operationally subordinated?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is it logical that a battalion commander, based on the information given to him by the Military District Commander, in the preparation for an operation as regards the deployment of forces, axis of attack, and everything else that may come his way as information, drafts his implementation order precisely in detail, describing everything referred to in item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in none of those orders that I could find in terms of before and during Operation Storm that come to you and say, Go to your commander to whom you're daily operationally subordinated to get a plan or get instructions on what you're supposed to do. And if I could show you another document in this line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3134, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, an order from you to all the military police units, dated the 2nd of August, and these are now specific instructions: Military police treatment of foreigners and media representatives when they are visiting a protected building or when they want to enter areas of war operations. You order: "While performing everyday military police tasks concerning security, patrol service check-points are in contact with foreigners. For the purpose of the same military police member's treatment of the above-mentioned persons, I hereby order..." It says: "MP members who are performing tasks are obliged to enter the aforementioned and visitors book." Paragraph number 2: "In the event that foreigners are caught near a secured building (at a place where they're not supposed to be), taking photographs of the secured building or observing it, military policemen should approach them, take away the camera, fill out an LS 01 form, and hand the person [sic] over together with the camera or video camera to a SIS officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Turn the page in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 talks about confiscating photographs and videos. Paragraph 4: "Military policemen at the check-points shall fill out an LS 01 form for all foreigners and allow them into the area of war operations only with the approval of the SIS officer ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I have one more document to show, but if I could tender this. It's a 65 ter exhibit, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Tender it. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Then, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D1282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could have Exhibit D269, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is, again, an order of yours from the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see that this is the order on the work of the military police issued on the 3rd of August. Now, you ordered all the military police units -- and if we could, for example, go to paragraph 1.1. Actually, paragraph 1 talks about making contact with the police administration chiefs and the commanders of the police stations - these are the civilian police - in the zones of responsibility and agree on joint work on tasks. 1.1 is establish strict check-points. 1.2 -- if I could turn the page first, thank you - follow the advance of the RH armed forces in the depth of the liberated territory. 1.3: In populated places by means of joint patrols, ensure law and order and everything else as listed in point 1.2. The RH MUP will take over the security of vital buildings. 1.4: At bigger intersections in liberated areas, establish joint check-points in order to regulate traffic and provide security for HV and civilian columns. It goes on, and I won't repeat it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page and go to paragraph 3, numbered paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, you ordered: "Women, children, and the elderly from liberated areas shall be handed over by members of the military police to the nearest police station in the liberated area of the Republic of Croatia or to the police station in the free territory of the Republic of Croatia with a record being made of the persons handed over and signed by the person taking them over in the RH MUP police station. "VP unit commanders shall brief all levels of command in VP units and all members of the military police on this order during the night and ensure that it is implemented." And it's signed by you, copied to many, including the Military District Commanders. Now, would you agree with me that many of the points that you have in this order are points that are covered by Article 10 of the rules of the military police? The tasks. The tasks that you've outlined here are tasks identified in Rule 10 of the Rules of the military police; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 10? It refers to the scope of authority and the tasks of the military police, enumerating the tasks and duties of the military police. However, in the preamble, it is also mentioned that joint action be introduced in terms of tactics and methodology that would be applied across all MP units. I also asked for energetic efforts across all units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, and that's the point I tried to make with you about an hour ago, maybe less, about the centralised system and getting uniform application in the field of what needed to get done. But things like what military police were supposed to with civilians that they encountered or confiscating cameras and video recorders or setting up check-points, coordinating with the civilian police, those are all tasks under Article 10 that you ordered pursuant to your powers under Article 8; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. But we are not talking about micro-locations of the check-points. I don't know what the pace of advancement was to be. This was all to be provided in daily operational contact from the Military District Commander or some other organisational part of the Croatian army and followed upon. What I prescribed was a unified methodology and tactics of activity, joint action, energetic efforts as well as cooperation with the colleagues from the Ministry of Interior. All of those things were agreed upon at the strategic level. When you showed the first order that had to do with reporters, civilians, and others, that was ordered by the assistant minister for security and intelligence affairs, Mr. Rebic. Based on information he received from SIS and political affairs officers about uncontrolled entry of journalists and civilians, some of them were killed or injured. I can only recall -- I can recall one example of a BBC journalist who was killed. The second order had to do with the meeting which had been held at the highest level with our colleagues from the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's take two documents right now and see if we can admit them into evidence before we break for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have 65 ter 437, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is the order issued by the 72nd Military Police Battalion commander pursuant to the order we just saw on the screen. Essentially -- we don't need to go through it point by point because essentially what Mr. Budimir, the commander, did was copy your order, and he says he's acting pursuant to the order issued by you and passes that order down to his subordinate companies in the 72nd Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn the page, please. One more page, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You can see in the original that Commander Budimir doesn't copy the Military District Commander on what he's ordering. He gets your order and he executes it. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can just have a moment. Mr. Registrar, if I could have -- actually, if I could tender that right now, Mr. President. It's a 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This document, I'm informed, appears on a Bar table list for which I agreed that the -- Mr. Registrar would assign provisionally numbers, and that has been sent to the OTP for verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: For the record, we have no objection to the admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's already on the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At the risk of calling up another one that's on the Bar table list, Mr. Registrar, if could I have 65 ter 380, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report prepared by the company commander, Mr. Grancaric, of the military police company in Zadar, and he is reporting on the 4th that there was a meeting held on the 3rd of August, 1995, on the premises of the 3rd Company of the 72nd Military Police Battalion with Major Ivan Juric who issued certain orders in connection with the HV's activities in the zone of responsibility of the Zadar operations group: "After receiving tasks, I established contact with the commander of the operations group, Colonel Mladen Fuzul; commander of the 134th Home Guard Regiment, Major Cerina; chief of the SIS -- sorry, of the security subcentre of the Zadar SIS, Mr. Turkovic; and chiefs of the Zadar-Knin police administration." Now, in the December 1994 exhibit that I showed you earlier, one of the points was that they were, in the 72nd MPs, subordinated to the local highest-ranking commander, and at the end of the document it said that they were also required to coordinate with the police -- the civilian police and the SIS. And Mr. Grancaric here appears to be acting, he says, pursuant to orders that were issued to him by Major Juric, which was the person, as you've labelled him, your eyes and ears in the field, and you testified the person to whom you delegated some of your authority under Rule 8. He went then, and according to him, he established contact with the Commander Fuzul of the operative group Zadar. Now, is this an example of when we talk about or use phrases like vertical subordination and horizontal coordination, that he received his orders that went from Major Juric whose line went directly to you, but he's working with the local highest-ranking commander, Mr. Fuzul, to accomplish the regular military police tasks, the daily police tasks that a local commander may need to use the military police for?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit, I don't understand the gist of your question. On the 3rd of August, the highest-ranking officer of the Croatian army became the commander of operative group Zadar, and that is Colonel Fuzul. The commander of the military police company, Mr. Grancaric, established contact with the then-highest-ranking commander, conveyed to him what he had received as a written order from his battalion commander, and we have already seen that, and also what -- what Major Juric had told him. I don't know what Major Juric had told him, what orders he had issued to him. You'd have to ask Mr. Juric that, but I assume he only explained orally the order which the commander of the 72nd Battalion actually copied from my order. Everything else Mr. Grancaric, the company commander, in contact with the operative group chief, the chief of the SIS, and others did, and this is acting according to the rules. He was acting according to the rules and according to the order issued by the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We agree on that. But what I'd like to -- what we're interested in here is -- and if I can put to you this way, and it's a hypothetical, but Mr. Grancaric gets an order -- I'm going to assume that he received the order that you issued on the 3rd about check-points and where civilians were supposed to be taken, et cetera, and he is then also meeting with Mr. Fuzul who is the operations group commander and who is by no means in your chain of command. Now, am I right to say that if Commander Fuzul issued an order to Mr. Grancaric and said, You are ordered to ignore General Lausic's order, we are not setting up any check-points anywhere, that would have been an unlawful order issued by Mr. Fuzul; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I don't like answering hypothetical questions; and second, Mr. Grancaric, the company commander, would not be failing to obey my orders but the orders of his commander, the commander of the 72nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, you at your level, you insist that your orders when you issue them, like you did on the 3rd, are implemented all the way down; correct? I mean, if we were to look at military structure, if the commander below you doesn't execute the order, we have a problem; right? Let me also put a little twist on it. You said the 72nd MP commander. What Mr. Grancaric reported was not that he got the order from the 72nd Military Police Battalion commander, but that he got the order from Major Juric. And again, let me ask the question, or put it to you this way: Colonel Fuzul could not issue an order that would contradict the order that you passed down, whether it went through Major Juric or whether it went through Mr. Budimir; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a military police task?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The tasks that you ordered that we looked at, those documents right now. Let me repeat it again. For example, setting up check-points. I used that as an example.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Fuzul could not issue an order that would contradict your order to set up check-points; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he should issue the order that check-points not be set up? But the commander of the battalion had to carry out my order, setting up check-points. The micro-locations and everything else would come from the -- from Grancaric, in this case, and he would get it from the commander of the operative group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Last question for the day, and it's not only the commander of the 72nd MP that had to carry out your order. It was Major Juric that also had to carry out your order that you issued to him; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't think that is precisely a correct recap of what the witness was saying about who had -- which orders had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, let me be clear. You issued orders to Major Juric, and we'll look at them tomorrow. Those orders that you issued to Major Juric, they had to be carried out; correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issues had been -- the orders had been issued. If you don't expect your orders to be carried out, it's better not to issue them. You expect an order you issue to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's it for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Mr. Lausic, I give you -- could you please keep your earphones on when I give you again the instruction not to speak with whomever or to communicate in any way with anyone in relation to your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. We'd like to you back tomorrow in the afternoon in this same courtroom at a quarter past 2.00. We adjourn for the day, and we --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. Just very quickly, two matters I have been asked to place on record, that the Prosecution's two Bar table submissions were distributed via e-mail to everyone, and also I wanted to report to the Court that I do think 3343 I believe can be found at the very bottom of that Excel spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I failed, I believe, to tender the exhibit on the screen. I think it's a 65 ter as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe that's on the pending list and there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1283 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Tieger, you must have a Excel sheet different from mine. We'll not spend more time on it in court at this moment. We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, the 29th of January, quarter past 2.00, this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
